title: When the Money Stops: How Cuts to International Aid Are Hurting Global Health
label: 27 October 2026 · Global Health inquiry
summary: Committee members questioned health practitioners, researchers and UN staff about sudden cuts in donor funding—especially US aid—and how those cuts have disrupted services for HIV, sexual and reproductive health, maternal care, nutrition and infectious disease surveillance. Witnesses described immediate service interruptions, staffing losses, data problems, rising risks of infectious disease spread and a political backlash against rights-based services. They also suggested practical steps: protect core services, invest in data and diagnostics, support local organisations, expand private-sector partnerships, and maintain multilateral support while keeping some direct bilateral funding.

chapters.title: The sudden funding shock
chapters.takeaway: Abrupt donor cuts—especially from the US—left clinics, staff and community programmes suddenly without money and created panic.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: We’re starting the inquiry into global health. Please introduce yourselves briefly and the organisations you represent.

turns.speaker: Jerop Limo
turns.text: I run a Kenyan youth HIV organisation in Nairobi that supports adolescents living with HIV—helping them get medicines and psychosocial support beyond what clinics provide.

turns.speaker: Dr Natasha Kaoma
turns.text: I lead Copper Rose in Zambia, a youth-led, women-led group working on reproductive health, mental health and economic opportunities for young people.

turns.speaker: Abadi Assefa
turns.text: I’m Executive Director of the Family Guidance Association of Ethiopia, a long-standing family planning NGO working across clinics, public services and with displaced people.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Jerop, what did you see when donor funding was cut?

turns.speaker: Jerop Limo
turns.text: The cuts hit like a shock. Young people texted me in panic: 'We’re going to die.' Clinics, community services and patient-friendly providers we’d relied on suddenly disappeared or changed overnight.

turns.speaker: Jerop Limo
turns.text: Kenya moved to ‘integration’—putting HIV and other services into one primary care system. That sounds sensible on paper but can’t be done overnight. The result has been confusion and people getting lost from care.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Did the Kenyan Government know this was coming?

turns.speaker: Jerop Limo
turns.text: No. We had even worked with government on sustainability plans in 2024, but neither civil society nor government expected such a rapid withdrawal.

turns.speaker: Dr Natasha Kaoma
turns.text: In Zambia the effect was similar: donor funding covered most HIV and sexual health programming. When it dropped we lost community outreach, standalone sexual health centres and preventive work that reached hundreds of thousands.

turns.speaker: Dr Natasha Kaoma
turns.text: A modelling study suggested tens of thousands of preventable deaths from short service interruptions; longer disruptions could be catastrophic—especially for children.

chapters.title: What fell apart: clinics, staff and rights
chapters.takeaway: Services, trained staff and data systems collapsed in many places; at the same time political pushback narrowed the language and scope of reproductive rights.

turns.speaker: Brian Mathew
turns.text: Natasha, what were the immediate consequences for communities and for sustaining past gains?

turns.speaker: Dr Natasha Kaoma
turns.text: We lost scale: programmes that once reached 200,000 people fell to tens of thousands. Staff were laid off—UNAIDS estimated many thousands lost jobs—and data systems hosted on donor servers became inaccessible.

turns.speaker: Dr Natasha Kaoma
turns.text: That’s not just numbers. It means fewer community workers to fight stigma, fewer clinics, and less prevention—so gains on HIV targets and child services can slip back.

turns.speaker: Tracy Gilbert
turns.text: Have you seen political or ideological resistance to your work, and how has that affected services?

turns.speaker: Jerop Limo
turns.text: Yes. In Kenya political statements narrowed the space for talking about rights. Organisations were attacked and programmes on safe abortion or youth sexuality education were constrained.

turns.speaker: Dr Natasha Kaoma
turns.text: In Zambia the word 'rights' has been removed from official documents; 'gender' language is being replaced. That creates fear—organisations spend energy surviving rather than advocating.

turns.speaker: Abadi Assefa
turns.text: In Ethiopia we’ve seen external actors pushing family-values agendas and engaging parliamentarians and religious leaders. Lack of transparency on agreements worries us because it can change policies.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Abadi, what did the cuts mean for your services?

turns.speaker: Abadi Assefa
turns.text: We lost a big chunk of our budget, had to reduce staff and withdraw services from many facilities. In some areas girls have missed contraceptives after sexual violence and some young people share antiretroviral drugs because of stockouts.

chapters.title: How governments and groups are responding — risks and possible solutions
chapters.takeaway: Governments are trying to fill gaps through integration, domestic funding and private sector engagement; witnesses urged investment in data, diagnostics, local organisations and workforce.

turns.speaker: David Mundell
turns.text: Are there any positive changes or opportunities from this shock?

turns.speaker: Dr Natasha Kaoma
turns.text: Opportunities exist: use existing systems rather than rebuild, strengthen health insurance, scale private-sector provision of medicines, and invest in digital training to retain workforce skills.

turns.speaker: Jerop Limo
turns.text: A positive is that governments woke up to over-reliance on donors and some are prioritising health and integrating services. But integration must protect specialist, patient-friendly community services.

turns.speaker: Abadi Assefa
turns.text: Ethiopia is pushing country ownership and domestic resource mobilisation: small taxes and private sector partnerships are being explored and civil society is urged to diversify income.

turns.speaker: Noah Law
turns.text: How should the UK’s Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO) help local groups find private partners and develop data systems?

turns.speaker: Dr Natasha Kaoma
turns.text: Start with data: fund country-level data to show where gaps are. Offer blended finance for proven local businesses, and support data protection laws so health data can be used safely for digital and AI tools.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Monica, what does UNFPA do and how has the UK supported you?

turns.speaker: Monica Ferro
turns.text: UNFPA focuses on family planning, maternal health, ending gender-based violence and demographic data. The UK is a major donor and backs our supplies partnership that gets contraceptives and maternal supplies to many countries.

turns.speaker: Dr Kirrily de Polnay
turns.text: From MSF’s perspective, when primary care, prevention and labs fail the sickest people end up in our hospitals. That’s costlier and more complex care. We ask the UK to protect funding for nutrition and frontline services.

turns.speaker: Monica Harding
turns.text: Do people in donor countries still support international health spending?

turns.speaker: Monica Ferro
turns.text: Yes. The UK public donates and responds to appeals for crises and maternal health; public generosity is strong and often increases when governments cut funding.

chapters.title: Research, diagnostics and the multilateral vs bilateral debate
chapters.takeaway: Cuts to research and lab funding risk worse outbreaks and antimicrobial resistance; witnesses warned that relying only on multilaterals risks losing direct partnerships and local labs.

turns.speaker: David Taylor
turns.text: Jeanne, how have research and diagnostics been affected?

turns.speaker: Dr Jeanne Salje
turns.text: Overnight grant stops left labs and trials unable to operate. For diseases like TB that means interrupted treatment, more transmission and rising drug resistance. Loss of funding for lab networks harms outbreak detection.

turns.speaker: Dr Jeanne Salje
turns.text: We need sustained funding for reagents, trained staff and regional networks—not just machines in a room—to detect outbreaks early and prevent spread.

turns.speaker: Brian Mathew
turns.text: Is the move to put more UK money into multilaterals a problem for your work?

turns.speaker: Dr Jeanne Salje
turns.text: Yes, if it replaces direct, long-term research partnerships. Programmes like Newton and GCRF helped scientist-to-scientist links that build local capacity; losing those reduces real partnerships.

turns.speaker: Dr Kennedy Uadiale
turns.text: From Malawi: lab and surveillance funding cuts (including the Fleming Fund) left hospitals unable to produce lab results for months and stalled AMR policy meetings. Rapid affordable surveillance approaches the UK supports could help.

turns.speaker: Noah Law
turns.text: What should multilaterals do better?

turns.speaker: Dr Kennedy Uadiale
turns.text: Support standards, sustain in-country technical support and keep technical working groups running. The WHO and UNICEF need backing to maintain national action plans and emergency preparedness.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Any final specific asks for the UK Government?

turns.speaker: Dr Kirrily de Polnay
turns.text: Protect existing nutrition and primary care funding, keep supporting local partners, and maintain accountability for money routed through multilaterals.

turns.speaker: Monica Ferro
turns.text: Use the UK’s diplomatic voice to defend rights-based services, back local actors, and invest in maternal health as a development and humanitarian priority.

turns.speaker: Jerop Limo
turns.text: Invest in community workers, make the social health insurance real by ensuring services actually work, and reconnect with civil society as an essential partner.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you all. This evidence underlines the fragility of progress when funding stops, the political pressures on rights, and the practical fixes we should press for: protected core funding, diagnostics and data, support for local partners, workforce investment and careful multilateral engagement.
